prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks meet the mandate as I read it: an original invention (the magic-wavelength lattice, which removes motional and light-shift errors while interrogating many atoms at once) followed by an experimental realization that is verified rather than merely promised. Independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) now reproduce and compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, so this is the stable, repeatedly confirmed kind of result I want to be 'absolutely sure' about. It is also a new tool that opens a door: relativistic geodesy, tests of constant variation and dark-matter searches are being done with it. Seven of eight members put it in their top three, including members with quite different fields, which tells me the case does not depend on one member's specialty. Katori holds the invention and first demonstration, Ye the record accuracy and many-body control; a two-name prize is clean and leaves room in the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to earlier prizes: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable, and the 2012 prize covered ion control and the Al+ optical clock. A reader could see the lattice clock as an extension of recognised work rather than a new discovery, and the committee has to avoid the 'second, better version' trap I have warned about publicly. It is also precision engineering more than a new phenomenon, and part of its promised impact (redefinition of the second) has not yet happened. Finally, other contributors (Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde, Derevianko) are outside the credited names, so the attribution line must be written carefully.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B005 first but raises whether the prize should be tied to the clock invention or to the broader frequency-comb and metrology lineage already honoured in 2005, and says he cannot verify the priority chronology between Katori's proposal and parallel ideas.
responses.response: I would keep the citation narrowly on the lattice clock, not on metrology in general, precisely so that it does not read as a repeat of 2005. The comb is a tool the clock uses; the new element is the magic-wavelength trapping that lets many neutral atoms be probed without motional or Stark shifts. On chronology, this is exactly the point on which the committee must verify the original papers (Katori's 2001-2003 proposal against the first Sr lattice clock measurements and Ye's later comparisons) before it is final. I do not think the uncertainty changes the ranking, but it belongs in the verification list.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B035 (IceCube) first on the strength of detector development leading to a new observational window, and ranks B005 second, noting that Hall/Hänsch (2005) and Wineland (2012) reduce novelty marginally while the invention remains distinct.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of the overlap and I share his weight on instruments that open a window. Where I differ is on maturity and attribution for IceCube. Individual source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still at the few-sigma level, the discovery is the work of a collaboration of several hundred people, and any three names would shortcut AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND history. I ranked it sixth for that reason; it is a real discovery, but I cannot yet be sure the right three people are identified. The lattice clock has a sharper inventor line and repeated cross-laboratory confirmation. I would keep IceCube on the list for a later year rather than push it now.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks KPZ first and B005 third, and asks whether the committee sees the lattice clock as precision engineering or as a discovery in the Nobel sense; he also stresses that topological insulators (B020) sit close to the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I take the first question seriously, because I use the discovery-or-invention wording myself. The statutes say 'discovery or invention', and the lattice clock is an invention with a measured outcome that nobody could previously obtain, which I think satisfies it better than a method paper would. I do share his reservation on B020 and would not support it ahead of B005 for the same overlap reason. I cannot judge KPZ on the experimental side from the opening files: Mehlig himself says experimental realisations are fewer and noisier than the theory, and my criterion is that the original experiment be verified.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B015 (optical-lattice quantum simulation) first and B005 second, and asks whether the committee should wait for the SI second redefinition as a marker of impact.
responses.response: I would not wait. The impact is already demonstrated by the clock comparisons and the new measurements, and the redefinition is a policy timetable set by metrology bodies, not a test of the physics. On B015 I respect the case and the maturity, but the four-name credit versus a three-seat limit is a real problem, and Esslinger versus Zoller is not something the opening files resolve; Lindroth and Johansson himself both flag this. I would hold B015 as a strong alternative only if B005 stalls on attribution, not ahead of it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Primary-source verification of priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and parallel lattice-clock ideas and early demonstrations.
Whether Takamoto, Ludlow or another early contributor has a claim that the two-name configuration would overlook.

My own preferred candidate B051 (aberration-corrected electron optics) has the Krivanek/STEM-corrector credit question unresolved and has so far no support from colleagues, so I treat it as an alternative rather than as my first choice.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I do note that my own field of electron microscopy makes me an interested party on B051 (Rose, Urban, Haider), and the profile lists IFSM and Japanese microscopy and University of Tokyo ties (Katori's clock work is associated with Tokyo and RIKEN), which are general and not specific to him; I would still flag it and recuse on B051 if it advances, and I share a Chalmers affiliation with Johansson.
